Hyperopia

A 201-child bidirectional cohort study found faster axial elongation in children receiving red-light treatment than in comparison children. The observational design does not establish causation.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

A 201-child bidirectional cohort study found faster axial elongation in children receiving red-light treatment than in comparison children. The observational design does not establish causation.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact hyperopia category contains one 2026 human publication: a bidirectional cohort study of 201 children. No randomized trial, independent replication, animal model, or laboratory study is listed. The observation concerns eye growth in hyperopic children, not treatment of myopia. Li et al. 2026

Human and clinical evidence

The cohort report compared axial elongation in children receiving low-level LED red-light therapy with a comparison group. The treated group showed faster axial elongation, with an interaction estimate of +0.082 mm per year and a 95% confidence interval from 0.042 to 0.122 mm per year. The report also describes reduced interocular axial-length differences in anisometropic cases. Because treatment was not randomly assigned, baseline differences, treatment selection, and other confounders may account for some or all of the association. The study does not show that red light safely or effectively corrects hyperopia.

Animal evidence

No hyperopia-specific animal treatment study is listed in this exact category.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No in-vitro or ex-vivo study directly addressing hyperopia was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The source identifies low-level LED red light, but a standardized clinical dose or independently reproduced schedule is not established by this single cohort. The results apply to the studied pediatric population and should not be transferred to adults, different refractive groups, or other red-light devices without comparative evidence.

Interpretation

This is a preliminary observational signal with an outcome that may be clinically important. It does not establish causality, benefit, or a preferred protocol. Randomized studies and independent safety assessment are needed before drawing conclusions about red-light use in hyperopic children.

Publications and records1 publication: 1 human bidirectional observational cohort study with 201 children.

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Evidence is one 2026 bidirectional cohort study of 201 children, without random assignment or independent replication. Treated children showed faster axial elongation than comparison children. The association warrants careful scrutiny but cannot determine causation or define a treatment benefit. Unmeasured differences may still influence the observed association.

Publication and study types

  • It is not randomized and has no independent replication in the mapped category.
  • The participant cohort is described within the single publication.
  • No animal, in-vitro, or ex-vivo studies are listed.
